passages.t: ‘Your sons like olive shoots around your table’: the twin of Psalm 127
passages.happening:
Psalm 128 begins, “A song of ascents. Blessed are all who fear the LORD, who walk in His ways!” (verse 1).

It describes the good life of such a person. “For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours” (verse 2). “Your wife will be like a fruitful vine flourishing within your house, your sons like olive shoots sitting around your table” (verse 3). “In this way indeed shall blessing come to the man who fears the LORD” (verse 4).

Then it turns to a blessing, as a priest might speak it. “May the LORD bless you from Zion, that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life” (verse 5), “that you may see your children's children” (verse 6). It ends, “Peace be upon Israel!” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 127 said work and family are in vain unless the LORD builds them. Psalm 128 shows what it looks like when he does. Read the two together.

‘The fear of the LORD’ is not terror but awe and trust that shape how a person walks, as the note on Psalm 111 explains.

To eat what you have grown was not a given in that world. Drought, locusts, raiders and taxes could take a harvest before a family ever ate it. So verse 2 is a real gift.

The vine and the olive were two of the great gifts of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8). A vine gave grapes and wine. An olive tree gave oil for food, light and medicine. Olive trees can live a very long time, and young shoots spring up around the base of an old tree. That may lie behind the picture of children around the table: green and growing, around a rooted parent.

The blessing in verses 5 and 6 joins the home to the city. A family's good and Jerusalem's good belong together. Zechariah pictured the same hope: “Old men and old women will again sit along the streets of Jerusalem” (Zechariah 8:4), and “the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there” (Zechariah 8:5).
passages.later: Jesus said, “I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit” (John 15:5). Paul told fathers, “do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).
passages.hard: Does this psalm promise that everyone who fears God will have a happy family and plenty to eat? No. It describes the way God's world is meant to work, and it ends as a prayer (‘May the LORD bless you’), which treats these good things as gifts, not wages. Job feared God and lost his children and his wealth. The care lines in the note on Psalm 127 are for this psalm too: a home without a spouse or children, or a single person, is not less blessed in God's eyes, and childlessness is not a judgment from God.
passages.asks:
Psalm 128 is a picture of ordinary life made good: work that feeds you, a table with people around it, grandchildren, a city at peace. It asks you to notice these as gifts from God when you have them.

If your table looks different from the one in verse 3, the blessing in verse 5 is still for you: ‘May the LORD bless you from Zion.’ You may pray it over your own home, and over the homes around you.
